item.content:encoded:
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles llamaron de vuelta al lanzador Emmet Sheehan como parte de una serie de movimientos en el roster el domingo, y está previsto que el derecho se encargue de la mayor parte del juego en el cierre de la serie contra los Gigantes de San Francisco.
Las cuatro transacciones involucraron a lanzadores de los Dodgers. También llamaron de vuelta a Kyle Hurt, colocaron a Tarik Skubal en la lista de duelo y enviaron a Seth Halvorsen a Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Movimientos en el roster de los Dodgers
Jack Dreyer abrirá mientras los Dodgers buscan la barrida ante sus rivales del Área de la Bahía, antes de cederle el turno a Sheehan.
"Hoy estamos armando esto un poco con las opciones disponibles. Creo que se trata más de lo que, en nuestra opinión, le da a Emmet la mejor oportunidad", comentó el mánager Dave Roberts.
El jardinero derecho Kyle Tucker no estará en la alineación después de salir de la victoria del sábado por 10-4 debido a un lanzamiento foul que le pegó en la rodilla derecha.
Lesiones y esperanzas de regreso
Los Dodgers esperan ver pronto de regreso a Shohei Ohtani tras su primera estancia en la lista de lesionados desde que se unió al equipo en 2024. Podría ocurrir durante una serie de tres juegos contra los San Diego Padres que comienza la noche del martes. "Aún está en el aire, pero esa es nuestra esperanza", señaló Roberts.
Ohtani está en la lista de lesionados de 15 días por una inflamación en el bíceps derecho. También ha estado lidiando con molestias en la rodilla izquierda desde hace meses.
Expectativas sobre el regreso de Ohtani
Roberts cree que Ohtani llegará sin dolor a la última semana de la temporada regular, mientras los Dodgers presionan para asegurar un descanso y evitar la ronda de comodines.
"Creo que hay una diferencia entre molestia y dolor. ¿Está al 100 por ciento? Probablemente no. ¿Está mejor que hace una semana? Sí", manifestó Roberts.

Roberts also believes it’s important for Ohtani to get as many at-bats as possible once he returns to the f
item.content:encoded:
Dodgers Star Shohei Ohtani Could Return To Lineup On Wednesday Against Padres
Shohei Ohtani could make his return for the Los Angeles Dodgers sooner rather than later.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts provided an encouraging update on Ohtani, revealing that he could return as early as Wednesday and is expected to play every game down the stretch once activated.
Roberts also believes it’s important for Ohtani to get as many at-bats as possible once he returns to the field.
Through 130 games, Ohtani is batting .277 with 30 home runs, 80 RBIs, and a .902 OPS. While his offensive numbers rank among the league's elite, Ohtani won't return to the mound this season or during the playoffs as he focuses exclusively on hitting.
Regardless of his status on the mound, the plan remains to maximize Ohtani’s impact at the plate as much as possible. The Dodgers continue to hold firm control of the National League West with a 95-60 record and a nine-game lead in first place.
If Ohtani can return on Wednesday against the San Diego Padres, it will mark his first game back since Sept. 7. For a Dodgers team eyeing a historic three-peat, inserting Ohtani’s bat back into the lineup provides a massive boost heading into the postseason.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are currently taking on the San Francisco Giants in a weekend series.
With the NL West already wrapped up, the Dodgers are just a few wins away from locking up the No. 2 seed in the NL.
Before the Giants game on Sunday, LA announced its starter, with the anticipation that the contest would be a bullpen game.
Jack Dreyer Gets Start As Opener on Sunday
On Sunday, reliever Jack Dreyer will get the start against the Giants.
@UnderdogMLB revealed the news:
Dodgers: "9/20 M. Betts SS T. Edman CF T. Hernández RF F. Freeman 1B M. Rojas 2B M. Muncy 3B J. De Paula DH E. Hernández LF H. Feduccia C J. Dreyer SP"
Hunter Feduccia is doing the catching duties on Sunday afternoon.
@FabianArdaya wrote:
"Jack Dreyer is opening today. Emmet Sheehan has a locker. So does Kyle Hurt."
So, sounds like there could be some roster moves before Sunday's contest as well.
Taking a Quick Look at Jack Dreyer
Jack Dreyer has been a very solid reliever for the Dodgers over the past two seasons.
In 59.1 innings pitched with LA in 2026, Dreyer carries an ERA of 3.19 with 68 strikeouts.
Dreyer has logged 135.2 IP in his MLB career, and over that span, he holds an ERA of 3.05 with 142 Ks, a WHIP of 1.084, and a pitching record of 8-4.
It will be interesting to see how Dreyer can aid the Dodgers on Sunday, and how Dave Roberts handles the bullpen in the bulk outing.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers made a number of pitching moves ahead of Sunday’s series finale against the San Francisco Giants. Tarik Skubal, who started on Saturday, was placed on bereavement leave, which facilitated the return of Emmet Sheehan from Triple-A Oklahoma City. In addition, reliever Kyle Hurt was recalled and Seth Halvorsen optioned in a swap of right-handers in the bullpen.
Sheehan was just optioned on Monday and normally would have needed to stay in the minors for 15 days, but because he’s replacing a player on the bereavement list (or injured list or paternity list) that allows the right-hander to return early.
After getting sent down to Triple-A on August 3, Sheehan turned his season around, including winning Pacific Coast League pitcher of the month, and he allowed one run in 11 2/3 innings last week for the Dodgers before getting optioned to Oklahoma City so the Dodgers could use a fresh arm. In his last five outings — three in Triple-A, two with Dodgers — Sheehan has allowed only two runs in 29 innings with 39 strikeouts (36.4-percent strikeout rate) against only eight walks.
All 26 outings by Sheehan this season have been starts, but on Sunday he’ll follow an opener in left-hander Jack Dreyer. Sunday provides at least a practice run of Sheehan’s most likely role in the postseason, pitching in bulk relief.
“Emmet’s a part of the conversation,” manager Dave Roberts said Sunday, “but if there is a role in the postseason it would be out of the ’pen.”
Bereavement leave lasts for a minimum of three days and up to seven, so Skubal wouldn’t be activated until Wednesday at the earliest. But considering the left-hander just started on Saturday, don’t expect him to be activated until his start day, likely next weekend in San Francisco.
Halvorsen has allowed nine runs in 10 innings with the Dodgers, including three home runs, with six strikeouts and two walks. He pitched a scoreless inning on Saturday, which was his third appearance in four days.
Hurt pitched a scoreless inning for Oklahoma City on Friday, his only appearance in the last week. Since getting optioned on September 5, Hurt pitched in three games for Oklahoma City, all scoreless innings. This season with the Dodgers, Hurt has a 4.33 ERA and 3.84 xERA in 43 games, with 56 strikeouts and 23 walks in 43 2/3 innings.
Saturday was his 15th day on optional assignment in Triple-A, making Sunday his first day eligible to return from the minors.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Los Angeles Dodgers recalled pitcher Emmet Sheehan as part of a series of roster moves Sunday, with the right-hander set to handle the bulk of their series finale against the San Francisco Giants.
All four transactions involved Dodgers pitchers. They also recalled Kyle Hurt, placed Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list and optioned Seth Halvorsen to Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Jack Dreyer will start as the Dodgers go for the sweep against their Bay Area rivals before giving way to Sheehan, who is 5-8 with a 4.79 ERA in 22 games this season.
“Kind of piecing through the available options today,” manager Dave Roberts said. “I think it's just more of what gives Emmet, in our opinion, the best chance.”
Right fielder Kyle Tucker won't be in the lineup after coming out of Saturday's 10-4 victory because of a fouled pitch that went off his right knee. The early exit was described as precautionary, and Roberts felt it was worth giving him a day off, particularly with Tucker finding his stride after an erratic first season in Los Angeles. He is batting .429 with five homers, eight extra-base hits and 11 RBIs in his past 10 games.
The Dodgers expect to see Shohei Ohtani back soon after his first stint on the injured list since joining the team in 2024. It could come during a three-game series against the San Diego Padres that starts Tuesday night. “Still up in the air, but that’s our hope,” Roberts said.
Ohtani is on the 15-day IL with right biceps inflammation. He also has been dealing with left knee soreness for months.
Roberts believes Ohtani will be pain-free going into the last week of the regular season, with the Dodgers pushing to secure a bye to avoid the wild-card round.
“I think there's a difference between discomfort and pain,” Roberts said. “Is it 100%? Probably not. Is it better than it was a week ago? Yes. Honestly, I think that's just a better question for Shohei to give specifics. But I do think that when he's activated, it's going to be the best physical place he's been in in quite some time.”

item.content:encoded:
Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal is going on the bereavement list, manager Dave Roberts announced on Sunday.
The move came a day after Skubal suffered his worst start with the Dodgers, giving up four runs in five innings in Saturday’s 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants.
In his absence, Emmet Sheehan was called up from triple-A, returning in hopes of building off back-to-back strong starts earlier this month. He will follow opener Jack Dreyer on Sunday as the bulk pitcher for the Dodgers’ series finale with the Giants.
Roberts said Skubal would be away from the Dodgers for “a couple days.” No further information on his situation was available.
Skubal is a contender to be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter in the playoffs, after being acquired in a blockbuster deal at the trade deadline in August. Even after Saturday’s setback, in which he allowed eight hits and bemoaned his lack of fastball command, the left-hander is 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA in nine starts with the Dodgers this season.
The two-time Cy Young Award winner will anchor a postseason rotation also expected to include Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell (assuming he continues to recover from his recent groin injury).
The Dodgers also freshened up their bullpen on Sunday, swapping out right-handers was calling up Kyle Hurt and optioning Seth Halvorsen.
The team enters Sunday with the chance to not only sweep the Giants, but further lower their current magic number of four to secure a first-round bye in the playoffs.
They enter play on Sunday four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves for the No. 2 seed in the National League.

item.content:encoded:
Kyle Tucker has started to heat up at the perfect time for the Los Angeles Dodgers. Signed this past offseason to a massive four-year, $240 million deal, he spent most of the summer struggling at the plate and unable to string together any consistent production. Just when it seemed like he would get hot, he would slide right back into another cold stretch.
However, September has been a different story entirely for Tucker. Over 18 games this month, the 29-year-old has posted a .288 batting average, .397 on-base percentage, 1.075 OPS, six home runs and 13 RBIs, while striking out just seven times and walking 12. The discipline and production have both been at an elite level.
The Dodgers are on the verge of clinching a first-round bye in the National League, and Tucker's surge has undoubtedly been a big reason why.
During Saturday's win against the San Francisco Giants, Tucker fouled a ball off his right shin and appeared to be in some discomfort. He remained in the game and finished it, and manager Dave Roberts said afterward he did not expect it to be an issue moving forward.
However, Tucker was not included in Sunday's series finale lineup against San Francisco. Teoscar Hernandez shifted to right field with Enrique Hernandez taking over the vacated spot in left field.
Speaking with reporters pregame, Tucker continued to downplay the issue and revealed he did not undergo any further testing. "I feel fine," Tucker said, per Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic.
Kyle Tucker: “I feel fine.”
Said he didn’t get any further testing. Like he said yesterday, hit him on a different spot than where he broke his shin in 2024. https://t.co/8KvewI1fkA
Tucker has an injury history with his right shin, previously breaking it back in 2024 when he was with the Houston Astros.
However, this situation is nowhere near as serious, and he will look to return for Tuesday's series opener against the San Diego Padres. It is unclear if he will be available off the bench Sunday.

item.title: [MLB.com] One of the game's hardest throwers delivers ... a 32.6 mph HBP?
item.dc:creator: Brian Murphy

item.content:encoded:
One of the game's hardest throwers delivers ... a 32.6 mph HBP?
This browser does not support the video element.
No batter wants to be hit by a pitch, but if they are going to get plunked, they probably all want the pitch to be like the one that made contact with the Giants’ Drew Gilbert on Saturday against the Dodgers.
In the ninth inning of Los Angeles’ 10-4 victory, Dodgers reliever Seth Halvorsen threw a 1-2 pitch to Gilbert that hit the outfielder on his right thigh. But it probably didn’t leave a mark since the pitch registered at just 32.6 mph and bounced on its way toward the plate.
That makes it the slowest recorded pitch on a HBP in the pitch-tracking era (since 2008). It surpassed the previous record-holder, a 34.2 mph pitch from the Reds’ Jose Trevino that hit the Pirates’ Jake Mangum on May 2.
Halvorsen, who was optioned to Triple-A on Sunday among a series of Dodgers roster moves, is one of the game’s hardest throwers, with an average fastball velo of 98.9 mph. But he appeared to either slip or have one of his cleat spikes get caught in the mound. That took the right-hander completely out of his delivery, but he still lobbed the pitch toward home.
It’s been a big week for funny hit-by-pitches. Saturday’s blooper occurred one week after the Guardians’ Joey Cantillo hit the Twins’ Brooks Lee with a 39.9 mph offering.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dodgers make pair of roster moves to add pitchers before bullpen game
item.dc:creator: Blake Williams
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers recalled Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt, optioned Seth Halvorsen and placed Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list ahead of their series finale against the San Francisco Giants. Skubal and Halvorsen both pitched on Saturday in the victory. Skubal allowed four runs in five innings, showing a lot of frustration with his outing. He gave up eight hits and walked two while only striking out three. He has made nine starts for the Dodgers since being acquired from the Detroit Tigers
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers recalled Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt, optioned Seth Halvorsen and placed Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list ahead of their series finale against the San Francisco Giants.
Skubal and Halvorsen both pitched on Saturday in the victory.
Skubal allowed four runs in five innings, showing a lot of frustration with his outing. He gave up eight hits and walked two while only striking out three.
He has made nine starts for the Dodgers since being acquired from the Detroit Tigers and he is 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA in 55 innings. On the season, he is 11-7 with a 2.85 ERA in 25 starts.
The two-time Cy Young award winner has been in the Major Leagues seven seasons, posting a 65-44 record with a 3.04 ERA in 162 games (159 starts). He has 1,065 strikeouts in 918.1 innings while owning a 1.02 WHIP.
Skubal must be on the bereavement list for a minimum of three days and a maximum of seven days. It’s unclear why he was placed on bereavement leave, but the list is used if the player has a death or serious illness in their family.
Halvorsen tossed a scoreless inning with two strikeouts to close out Saturday’s game.
He made 11 appearances with the Dodgers, going 1-1 with an 8.10 ERA. Before joining the Dodgers, he appeared in 21 games for the Colorado Rockies this year, posting an 0-1 record with a 4.74 ERA.
He has made 86 Major League appearances for the Rockies (2024-26) and Dodgers (2026), and he is 4-5 with a 4.78 ERA and 72 strikeouts in 81 innings.
Dodgers add reinforcements for bullpen game
Sheehan returns after pitching six scoreless innings against the Miami Marlins last Sunday. He has gone 5-8 with the Dodgers in 2026, posting a career-high 22 starts, racking up 123 strikeouts in 107 innings and a 1.21 WHIP.
He is in his third season with the Dodgers, recording a 4.23 ERA with a 15-12 record in 50 games (45 starts).
The Dodgers needed a pitcher who could throw the bulk of the game on Sunday, and Sheehan is likely to fulfill that role.
Hurt returns for his fifth stint with the team and provides them with another fresh arm before the bullpen game. He has gone 4-1 with a 4.33 ERA this season and 56 strikeouts in 43.2 innings.
He has been with the Dodgers three seasons, compiling a 3.78 ERA with 62 strikeouts in 52.1 innings and a 4-2 mark.

item.title: [MLB.com] Skubal to bereavement list, Sheehan recalled among LA moves; Tucker out of lineup

item.description: LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers made a flurry of roster moves before Sunday afternoon's series finale against the Giants, placing left-hander Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list, recalling right-handers Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt from Triple-A Oklahoma City and optioning right-hander Seth Halvorsen. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers made a flurry of roster moves before Sunday afternoon's series finale against the Giants, placing left-hander Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list, recalling right-handers Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt from Triple-A Oklahoma City and optioning right-hander Seth Halvorsen.
The Dodgers also gave right fielder Kyle Tucker Sunday off after he fouled a ball off the lower knee/upper shin area on his right leg on Saturday night. Manager Dave Roberts does not think the soreness will become an ongoing issue for Tucker, who is expected back in the lineup on Tuesday.
Here's how these moves will impact the Dodgers on Sunday and beyond:
Skubal will be away from the team for "a couple days," Roberts said. Players may spend between three to seven days on the bereavement list, so Skubal might not miss his next start, which is projected to come on Friday in San Francisco.
"Some personal stuff going on," Roberts said, "but he's fine."
Skubal is 4-2 with a 2.95 ERA in nine starts since being dealt to L.A. ahead of the Trade Deadline.
Sheehan was set to pitch bulk innings on Sunday behind opener Jack Dreyer. The thought was that pitching Sheehan behind an opener could not only help him get deeper into the game, but also prepare him for a possible bullpen role in the postseason, which would be his only path to making the roster.
In his previous two starts for the Dodgers, Sheehan allowed one earned run across 11 2/3 innings. After a strong stint in Triple-A, he has looked to trend in the right direction in what has been an inconsistent season overall (5-8, 4.79 ERA).
Tucker has heated up at the end of the first season of his four-year, $240 million contract, which has been disappointing (his .728 OPS is on track to be a career-worst mark in a full season). Since Sept. 9, he's hitting 15-for-35 (.429) with five home runs and 35 total bases, his most in a 10-game span this season.
On Saturday, Tucker exited the game after six innings due to a combination of the hit-by-pitch and the lopsided score. He said he feels fine, but Roberts decided to give him an extra day to rest after Tucker had played the previous nine games without a day off.
"I feel like everyone's grinding at this point in the season," Tucker said. "But I'll be good with it."

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal moved to the bereavement list on Sunday, and will be there for a "couple of days," per Dave Roberts.
In corresponding moves, the Dodgers optioned Seth Halvorsen and recalled Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt.
BREAKING: Tarik Skubal will be away from the Dodgers for a couple days due to personal reasons ?
Seth Halvorsen has also been optioned and Kyle Hurt and Emmet Sheehan are back.
Skubal last pitched for the Dodgers on Saturday, and had a frustrating outing—his worst since donning a Dodgers uniform. He lasted just five innings, allowing four earned runs on eight hits while recording a season-low three strikeouts.
What Does Tarik Skubal's Absence Mean?
The left-hander's presence on the bereavement list doesn't impact the rest of the Dodgers' season, as he will likely be ready for his next turn through the rotation if he stays out for a couple of days as Roberts said.
That should be a huge relief for the Dodgers, who have quite a few injuries among their starters as the postseason nears. Shohei Ohtani, Roki Sasaki and Eric Lauer are all on the IL, leaving LA with limited options.
An injury or extended period of absence for any of their remaining starters would throw a wrench in their plans for the postseason.
Additionally, Skubal's track record since joining the team is fantastic—serving as one of their best starters since the beginning of August. He has a 2.95 ERA through nine starts, striking out 60 batters through 55 innings pitched.
What Roles Will Kyle Hurt and Emmet Sheehan Play?
Hurt and Sheehan are likely to jump straight into the action, as the Dodgers are running a bullpen game on Sunday.
Jack Dreyer is getting the start, but using Hurt and Sheehan—both of whom have experience handling bulk innings—afterwards is the Dodgers' most likely move.
The duo have bounced between Triple-A and MLB over the past few weeks, but could very well find a spot on the team if they perform well Sunday. Sheehan is in the midst of a fantastic run of form, and has capitalized on both of his MLB opportunities in Setpember.
He only allowed one earned run through 11.2 innings pitched over his last two starts, and is a real candidate to make the postseason roster despite his recent stays in the minors.
Before that, though, he'll have to perform in Sunday's game against the Giants, which begins at 1:10 p.m. PT.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers announced a major roster move ahead of Sunday's series finale against the San Francisco Giants.
The Dodgers have recalled right-handed pitchers Emmet Sheehan and Kyle Hurt from Triple-A. Sheehan will take down bulk innings on Sunday as LA looks to preserve the bullpen heading into the final week of the regular season.
As for the corresponding moves, left-handed pitcher Tarik Skubal was placed on the bereavement list and will be away from the team for "a couple days," per manager Dave Roberts. Additionally, right-hander Seth Halvorsen was optioned.
Dodgers Recall Emmet Sheehan, Kyle Hurt
Sheehan was surprisingly demoted this past week amid a dominant stretch of play.
Across his last two starts at the MLB level, Sheehan allowed just one run over 11.2 innings with 15 strikeouts.
“Man, Emmet’s been great. The last two have been fantastic,” Roberts said after he was sent down. “Emmet’s done everything he can do in his power to force our hand, which I love. ... The last two have been really good.”
Now, Sheehan is getting another opportunity to take down bulk innings and audition for a spot on the postseason roster. If he has another strong outing, he'll likely secure a spot in the postseason bullpen as a multi-inning option.
As for Hurt, he's been up and down multiple times this season. The right-hander has made 43 appearances at the big league level, compiling a 4.33 ERA with 56 strikeouts to 23 walks over 43.2 innings of work.
He's unlikely to factor into the team's October plans, but could take down innings over the final week of the regular season.
Dodgers Place Tarik Skubal on Bereavement List, Option Seth Halvorsen
Skubal will deal with a personal matter for the next couple days, but should be back in time to make one more start before the conclusion of the regular season.
He pitched on Saturday, allowing four runs over five innings with three strikeouts.
As for Halvorsen, he's made 11 appearances at the big league level for the Dodgers this season, accruing an 8.10 ERA with six strikeouts to two walks over 10 innings of work.
He was acquired by the Dodgers a couple weeks before the trade deadline in a three-player deal with the Colorado Rockies. He likely won't return to the big league club for the remainder of the year.

item.title: [New York Post] Kyle Tucker out of Dodgers lineup as new injury concern surfaces
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: Just as Kyle Tucker was finally starting to heat up, he became the latest Dodgers star to suffer a potential injury concern. On Sunday, Tucker was not in the Dodgers’ lineup for their series-finale against the San Francisco Giants, absent a day after he left Saturday’s game early following a foul ball off his right knee/shin area. The good news: Tucker insisted on Sunday that he felt fine and didn’t anticipate it causing ongoing problems. Still, manager Dave Roberts had said Saturday night he ex
item.content:encoded:
Just as Kyle Tucker was finally starting to heat up, he became the latest Dodgers star to suffer a potential injury concern.
On Sunday, Tucker was not in the Dodgers’ lineup for their series-finale against the San Francisco Giants, absent a day after he left Saturday’s game early following a foul ball off his right knee/shin area.
The good news: Tucker insisted on Sunday that he felt fine and didn’t anticipate it causing ongoing problems.
Still, manager Dave Roberts had said Saturday night he expected Tucker in the lineup on Sunday, depending on how the issue progressed.
Tucker initially suffered the injury in the third inning Saturday night, when a foul ball banged high enough up his leg it evaded his shin pad.
The four-time All-Star immediately went down in pain, and was checked out by Roberts and a trainer for several moments.
Initially, Tucker stayed in the game, drawing a walk (and racing around the bases to later score a run) in the fifth while playing out in right field until the seventh.
However, he appeared to be moving around somewhat gingerly after the injury, and was ultimately removed once the score got out of reach in the Dodgers’ eventual 10-4 win.
Postgame, Tucker didn’t seem overly concerned with the issue, saying he should be “good with it” and that the lopsided score was a factor in his precautionary removal.
“I feel like everyone is grinding at this point of the season,” he noted.
On Sunday morning, he echoed that sentiment, saying Roberts had informed him Sunday they were “just gonna at least give me the day.”
The Dodgers will have to hope the injury doesn’t impact Tucker’s recently resurgent performance. In his last 10 games, the $240 million outfielder has finally started to turn a corner, going 15-for-35 with five home runs, nine extra-base hits and 11 RBIs in that stretch.
In 2024, a similar foul ball left Tucker with a right shin fracture that sidelined him for three months.
However, he said this one hit in a different spot of his leg, while once again downplaying the potential severity of the problem.
“This was a little different,” he said. “I feel fine.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers kept right fielder Kyle Tucker out of their lineup for Sunday’s game after he exited Saturday’s win early.
Tucker fouled a ball off of his shin Saturday, and left the game shortly after. Manager Dave Roberts expected Tucker to return to the lineup Sunday, but the outfielder clearly isn’t fit to participate.
Who is Starting for the Dodgers?
The Dodgers are running a bullpen day on Sunday, and could have a few players fill in if needed. Jack Dreyer is getting the ball first for the Dodgers, making his second start of the season. He has a 3.19 ERA through 63 appearances with 68 strikeouts in 59.1 innings pitched.
Emmet Sheehan has a locker at Dodger Stadium as well, and could handle bulk for LA on Sunday.
Who is in the Dodgers’ Lineup?
Shortstop Mookie Betts remains in the leadoff spot for the Dodgers, and center fielder Tommy Edman shoots up the order to bat second. Left fielder Teoscar Hernandez bats third, and first baseman Freddie Freeman serves as the cleanup hitter.
Miguel Rojas enters the lineup as the second baseman and No. 5 hitter, and third baseman Max Muncy slides down the order to the No. 6 spot. Josue De Paula remains the team’s designated hitter, and following him are left fielder Kiké Hernandez and catcher Hunter Feduccia to round out the Dodgers’ lineup.
Dodgers Lineup vs. Giants
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Tommy Edman, CF
3. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
4. Freddie Freeman, 1B
5. Miguel Rojas, 2B
6. Max Muncy, 3B
7. Josue De Paula, DH
8. Kiké Hernandez, LF
9. Hunter Feduccia, C
Who is Starting for the Giants?
On the mound for the Giants is left-hander Matt WIlkinson, who will be making his seventh appearance of the year. He has a 4.58 ERA through 19.2 innings pitched, striking out 12 batters durign that time.
The rookie struggled in his first stint as a starter, transitioning to relief for his last two appearances and holding his opponents scoreless.
The Dodgers will look to break his scoreless streak in Sunday’s game, which begins at 1:10 p.m. PT.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees Birthday of the Day: Tom Tresh
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mearns
item.description: Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
item.content:encoded:
Although a familiar name to scholars of Yankees history (for lack of a better term), Tom Tresh did not have a long big-league career due to injuries and treatment of the time. Nonetheless, he was among the Bombers’ finest players of the 1960s and one of the last gasps of greatness from their vaunted farm system. As the team around him declined, Tresh continued to perform at a high level at multiple positions, making him a fan favorite and a valued final connection to those terrific teams of old.
Thomas Michael Tresh
Born: September 20, 1938 (Detroit, MI)
Died: October 14, 2008 (Venice, FL)
Yankees Tenure: 1961-69
September 1938 was a big month for the Tresh family, as patriarch Mike made his MLB debut with the Chicago White Sox on September 4th, and son Tom was born on September 20th. Mike Tresh spent 11 years catching for the South Siders, playing in over 1,000 games in the majors until ending his career in 1949 with Cleveland. He was named an All-Star by the Associated Press in 1945, the only year of the 20th century in which the Midsummer Classic wasn’t held (after the creation of the All-Star Game in 1933).
Tom Tresh spent some time living with his parents in an apartment in Chicago, but he went to school in Michigan, as his father’s career was over by then. At Allen Park High School in Detroit, he lettered in baseball, football, and basketball, and he later went to Central Michigan University in Mount Pleasant. His father’s prestigious job allowed him to gain some first-hand perspective on how clubhouses operated and what big-league living was like. He was even allowed to become a bat boy when his father briefly managed at Daytona Beach and Wausau, Wisconsin in 1951 and 1952, respectively.
MLB teams knew just how talented the younger Tresh was, and they kept a close scouting eye on him growing up. Mike and Doris Tresh wanted their son to go to college, but after a year at shortstop in Central Michigan, Tresh felt that he could not turn down a $30,000 offer from the New York Yankees. It was a lot of money for the time, the Yankees were baseball’s marquee team, and like many boys in the ’50s, Mickey Mantle was his idol. He recalled going to Tiger Stadium when the Yankees came to town and watching him intently from the upper deck in center field. Mike had even taught Tom how to switch-hit like Mantle.
Ultimately, Tresh was able to convince his parents to let him sign with the Yankees at age 19, assuring them that he would go back and finish his degree. He was on his way to joining his hero at Yankee Stadium.
Tresh was quick to impress in his first exposure to pro ball in 1958, as he hit .316/.435/.445 for the St. Petersburg Saints in 126 games of Class D ball. His pace slowed down upon a late-season promotion to the Double-A New Orleans Pelicans (no, not them), where the average player was seven years his senior.
It was around this time that Tresh met his idol for the first time, down in spring training. It was recalled in Jane Leavy’s book on Mantle, The Last Boy:
The first time he saw Mantle up close, Tresh was in an elevator during rookie camp in St. Pete--the doors opened and there he was. Though they stood eye to eye, Mantle seemed a thousand steps higher--a feeling Tresh never got over. “I never could see him as just one step higher than I was.”
After batting .246/.363/.415 in 133 games with the Binghamton Triplets in A-ball in 1960, the Yankees tested him at the minors’ highest level. There was no pressure to promote the young prospect, as the big-league club was in the midst of one of their greatest seasons in history, a 109-win romp to the World Series powered by Mantle and Roger Maris. Tresh had a superb year in his own right, hitting .315/.380/.428 in 141 games at shortstop with Richmond and taking home International League MVP honors.
As a reward of sorts, Tresh was tabbed for his MLB debut as a September call-up in ‘61. With another Rookie of the Year-turned-regular in Tony Kubek at shortstop ahead of him, it was hard to find time. Tresh did make it into nine games though, debuting on September 3rd as a pinch-runner and taking his first at-bat on September 16th in his hometown at Tiger Stadium. Tresh notched his first big-league hit in the first game of a doubleheader on September 26th against the Orioles. The huge story that day was Maris tying Babe Ruth with his 60th homer of the season, but Tresh played his part as well, singling to right field off Jack Fisher in the middle of a rally that put the Yankees in front.
Tresh was only technically part of a championship team in ‘61, but the next year, he truly earned his ring. An opportunity arose, as Kubek was recalled to the U.S. Army Reserve. Manager Ralph Houk entrusted the starting role at shortstop to Tresh over fellow infielder Phil Linz. It was the right call, as Tresh went on to an All-Star rookie campaign. He capably fielded the position in Kubek’s absence while hitting well from both sides of the plate. Tresh racked up 20 homers and a .286/.359/.441 triple slash, good for a 119 wRC+, Rookie of the Year honors, and even a 12th-place finish for MVP.
There was the potential for an awkward situation to arise when Kubek returned from the service in August, and Houk tasked Tresh with playing alongside Mantle in left field. In 573 minor-league games, Tresh had never manned the outfield, but he handled it with aplomb. Having previously made that same transition, Mantle even gave Tresh his glove, choosing to befriend and praise his potential future replacement rather than ignoring him, as Joe DiMaggio did to Mantle. Tresh knew Mantle had his flaws, but he loved him anyway and eventually nicknamed his son “Mickey” for him in 1964. (“What the fuck did you do that for?” Mantle later asked. He knew he was no idol.)
The Yankees won the pennant and played the San Francisco Giants in the World Series. Tresh had only just turned 24 and yet he didn’t appear to be fazed at all. He hit .321/.345/.464 in the seven-game series, leading the Yankees in hits and average. It wasn’t garbage time participation either, as his three-run homer in the eighth off Jack Sanford gave the Yankees a Game 5 victory,
Mike Tresh was in the stands at Yankee Stadium when Tresh hit that homer to win Game 5, crying tears of joy. His son had definitely made it.
A terrific one-handed catch by Tresh on a seventh-inning Willie Mays drive in Game 7 likely saved a run with the red-hot Willie McCovey on deck. The Yankees edged the Giants 1-0 to bring home their 20th championship.
Rather than suffering a sophomore slump in ‘63, Tresh had an outstanding year. He was on fire, hitting .269/.371/.487 with 25 dingers and a career-best 141 wRC+. Tresh was an All-Star for the second year in a row and again earned down-ballot MVP votes as the Yankees ran away with the AL pennant thanks to 104 victories. Tresh spent the year in the outfield and even manned center while Mantle missed a few months due to injury. Unfortunately, they had no answer for the overwhelming Los Angeles Dodgers pitching staff in the World Series. Tresh managed to take the seemingly untouchable Sandy Koufax deep late in Game 1, but like most of his team, he was otherwise quiet. They swept the Yankees away.
Houk moved up to the front office in 1964 and the popular Yogi Berra took over in the dugout. The Yankees won their fifth straight pennant, but it was as tough a climb to the top as the team of that era ever endured. They battled injuries and ineffectiveness from several positions, including Kubek at shortstop. Tresh remained a solid player, though he also saw his numbers slip. The Yankees faced a tough competitor in the Cardinals, and it was a tight seven-game series. Tresh slugged .636 and homered twice, including a game-tying blast off World Series MVP Bob Gibson in the ninth inning of Game 5.
It wasn’t enough, as the Cardinals prevailed and Berra was stunningly fired.
The Yankees pulled off a classic “if you can’t beat him, sign him” move for ‘65 by hiring Johnny Keane, who just beat them in the World Series. Kubek played poorly at shortstop and missed a lot of time, but Keane kept Tresh in the outfield, alternating him between relieving Mantle in center and playing left (there was even some right mixed in). To some extent, it paid off, as Tresh finished in the top 10 for AL MVP, won a Gold Glove, and showed no sign of ill-effect at the plate with a 136 wRC+. To another extent, it didn’t, as the team around him was not good; the Yankees fell below .500 for the first time in 40 years.
Despite the increasing effects of a pitching-heavy era, Tresh pulled off a career-high in home runs in ‘66, smacking 27 dingers in 151 games. That was one of the few highlights for the Yankees though, who were abysmal and dropped all the way to last place. Keane was fired and replaced by Houk in May, who moved Tresh to third base since he wanted to give a young Roy White time in the outfield. Tresh ended up splitting time between left and the hot corner. The Yankees appreciated his athleticism and Zobristian ability to handle basically any position, but it still mystified Tresh to a certain degree:
“I win Rookie of the Year as a shortstop and they move me to the outfield. Then I win a Gold Glove Award there in 1965 and they move me to third. I couldn’t figure out what position I was supposed to prove I could play.“
Although Tresh was only 28 entering the 1967 campaign, the second game of spring training was the beginning of the end. He popped his right knee while firing a throw across his body from left field to the cutoff man. Tresh was in serious pain and could barely walk; it was later revealed to be torn cartilage. Inexplicably, the Yankees told him that he should try to play on it rather than undergo surgery.
It was a disaster. Through some miracle, Tresh kept his numbers above league-average with a 106 wRC+, but his OPS dipped below .700 and he was a shadow of the defender he once was in left field. Tresh later recalled that his knee “gave out five more times” that year, undoubtedly affecting his future. He had surgery to repair the damage in the offseason (why he wasn’t simply shut down on a 90-loss team is a mystery), but the damage was done. Tresh was mostly a hobbling shortstop in ‘68 and his play only worsened in ‘69.
By then, the only other position players aside from Tresh remaining from the Yankees’ early ’60s glory were Joe Pepitone and catcher Jake Gibbs. Mantle, Maris, Berra, Kubek, Elston Howard, and Bobby Richardson were all gone. Tresh was miserable. The team was middling at best, and he could barely hit, let alone play shortstop. So he asked if the Yankees would trade him to the Tigers, where he could at least be close to home, not to mention play for the defending World Series champions. The Yankees acquiesced, and Tresh was dealt to Detroit on June 14th. The very next person to wear number 15 for the Yankees was a worthy heir: Thurman Munson.
Tresh remained primarily a shortstop and appeared in 94 games for the Tigers, batting .224/.305/.387 with 13 homers, a .692 OPS that was amusingly still good for a 92 wRC+ in the league-wide offensive malaise. While Detroit was a better team, there was still no competing with the 109-win juggernaut Orioles, who ran away with the AL East in the first year of divisional play.
Tresh had gone through another surgery on his knee in hopes of playing again in 1970. However, the Tigers told him that he would need to rehab in the minors, and Tresh had no intention of living that kind of life again, particularly with a wife and four kids at home. So Tom Tresh retired having played just eight games after his 31st birthday. His story was a warning sign about the dangers of dismissing injuries, but he had no regrets.
Even though Tresh was so talented before his injury that the Red Sox briefly considered a swap of him for Carl Yastrzemski, one can’t blame Tresh for his overall happiness about his career. He was a beloved teammate, a World Series champion, an All-Star, and an MVP candidate for baseball’s greatest franchise. At the time of his retirement, he was even in the Yankees’ all-time top 20 in homers at 140 (the recent offensive spike pushed him back to a tie for 34th as of 2026). Tresh had a fine life post-retirement too, as he did fulfill that college promise to his parents, even after his father’s passing in 1966.
Tresh earned his degree in physical education from Central Michigan in 1969, where he later served as an assistant baseball coach for 15 years and helped innovate a training tool for sliding and diving called the Slide-Rite. His son Mickey inherited the baseball gene, playing at Miami University of Ohio before going through four years in the minors as well with New York and Detroit. The younger Tresh even got a glimpse of the ascendance of one of the great successors to Tresh and Mantle in center: his 1988 Prince William Yankees teammate, 19-year-old Bernie Williams.
The bond between the Mantles and Treshes remained strong—the two Yankees were at a card show in Nashville when Mickey Tresh called to inform his father that he just had a boy of his own, who he named Tommy. Mantle celebrated with Tresh by ordering a $150 bottle of Dom Perignon, raising a toast to the lad, and later writing “Happy birthday Tommy, we had one for you. Mickey Mantle.” on the bottle.
That bottle could have sold for something valuable, as the glove Mantle gave to Tresh in 1962 was enough by itself to put a down payment on a cottage. Tom Tresh never sold it though; it meant too much to him, and he grieved as much as any of his teammates on the day Mantle passed away from liver cancer in 1995. Thirteen years later, Tresh suddenly left the world as well, as he died of a heart attack on October 14, 2008, not even a month after turning 70.
At least Tresh got to see the old Yankee Stadium one last time before it closed for good, as he was in attendance at the final Old-Timers’ Day. As always, the crowd gave him an ovation before he stepped to foul line one last time. Number 15 will always mean Thurman Munson, but it will also always be connected to Tommy Tresh, another fantastic Yankee.

item.content:encoded:
Joe Amalfitano and Charlie Hough Win Tommy Lasorda I Bleed Dodger Blue Award
LOS ANGELES – The Los Angeles Dodgers today named Charlie Hough and Joe Amalfitano as recipients of the Tommy Lasorda I Bleed Dodger Blue Award, an honor bestowed every year since 2022 to members of the Los Angeles Dodger community who embody the passion, enthusiasm and love for the Dodgers that the Hall of Fame manager possessed. The award will be presented today by Lasorda’s daughter Laura before the Dodgers’ 1:10 p.m. game against the San Francisco Giants, two days before what would have been Lasorda's 99th birthday.
Hough, 78, has spent 46 years in the Dodger organization as a player, coach and special assistant in the Baseball Operations department, dating back to his selection by the franchise in the eighth round of the June 1966 Amateur Draft. Making his MLB debut for Los Angeles in 1970, Hough pitched 799.2 innings in 401 games for Los Angeles with a 3.50 ERA, including 60 saves and a franchise record 204 relief appearances of at least two innings. Retiring from the Majors at age 46 in 1994 with the Marlins, he finished with a 216-216 career record and 2,362 strikeouts across 3,801.1 innings and 858 games, with a 3.75 ERA.
Amalfitano, 92, served 14 seasons as third-base coach on Lasorda’s staff from 1983-96, as well as Dodger senior adviser in baseball operations from 2002-04. Overall, Amalfitano amassed 67 seasons in professional baseball as a Major League player with the New York/San Francisco Giants, Houston Colt .45s and Chicago Cubs (1954-67), manager with the Cubs (1979-81) and front office executive. As a player, Amalfitano collected 418 hits across 10 seasons in the Majors.
The previous winners of the Lasorda award include longtime public relations executive Steve Brener (2025), Hall of Fame broadcaster Jaime Jarrín (2025), former catcher Steve Yeager (2024), longtime Minor League manager John Shoemaker (2023) and former Los Angeles City Councilmember Rosalind Wyman (2022).
The Los Angeles Dodgers franchise, with nine World Series championships and 26 National League pennants since its beginnings in Brooklyn in 1890, is committed to a tradition of pride and excellence. The Dodgers, baseball’s 2024 and 2025 back-to-back World Champions, are the reigning Sports Business Journal Sports Team of the Year, have been recognized as ESPN’s Sports Humanitarian Team of the Year and are dedicated to supporting a culture of winning baseball, providing a first-class, fan-friendly experience, and building a strong partnership with the community. With the highest cumulative fan attendance in Major League Baseball history and a record of breaking barriers, the Dodgers are one of the most cherished sports franchises in the world. Visit the Dodgers online at www.dodgers.com, follow them on Twitter @Dodgers and like them on Facebook at www.facebook.com/Dodgers. For media information, visit www.dodgerspressbox.com.

item.title: [si.com] Cam Schlittler Enters MLB History With Sandy Koufax, Bob Gibson During Cy Young Race
item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski; Unknown
item.description: New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler has joined two Hall of Fame pitchers in the record books after what was likely his second-to-last start of the 2026 regular season. item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler has joined two Hall of Fame pitchers in the record books after what was likely his second-to-last start of the 2026 regular season.
Schlittler tossed six innings against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, giving up one earned run on three hits and three walks while striking out six. This was the 24th time this season the right-hander hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start, tying Hall of Famers Bob Gibson and Sandy Koufax for the second-most such starts since 1920, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs. Koufax is also at the top of that list with 25 starts in which he gave up no more than one earned run, so the Yankees hurler will have a chance to tie the Dodgers legend again in his final regular-season outing of the year.
This stat is just the latest example of how truly dominant Schlittler has been this season. In fact, some fans have been debating whether the hard-throwing righty could be a legitimate contender for the 2026 American League MVP. At the very least, the young pitcher has made a strong case for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
Has Cam Schlittler already done enough to claim the AL Cy Young?
With just one week left in the 2026 MLB regular season, the two pitchers with the best chance to win the American League Cy Young Award are Schlittler and Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease. Schlittler now has an AL-leading 1.94 ERA in 32 starts this year, racking up 234 strikeouts in 190 2/3 innings. Meanwhile, Cease leads the American League with 239 strikeouts and has a 2.40 ERA in 169 innings.
In Cease's most recent start on Friday, the 30-year-old threw just 2 2/3 innings and walked six batters. He had an MRI done on his shoulder Saturday night and is no longer expected to make his next scheduled start on Wednesday, according to The Athletic's Mitch Bannon. While the Toronto hurler could pitch again later in the week, this may impact his chances of making a late push for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
As things stand, Schlittler seems like the frontrunner for this year's AL Cy Young Award. But the final week of the regular season could play a last-minute role in the eventual outcome.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Edwin Díaz shares encouraging update on feel for pitching since returning
item.dc:creator: Matt Borelli
item.description: Edwin Díaz hasn’t lived up to expectations in his first season with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he is hoping to finish the year on a good note and perhaps emerge as a bigger factor during the playoffs. Since returning from the 15-day injured list over the weekend, the right-hander has thrown two scoreless innings against the San Francisco Giants. In those appearances, he allowed just two baserunners and collected four strikeouts. “Yeah, 100%,” Díaz said when asked if he feels as good as he has
item.content:encoded:
Edwin Díaz hasn’t lived up to expectations in his first season with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but he is hoping to finish the year on a good note and perhaps emerge as a bigger factor during the playoffs.
Since returning from the 15-day injured list over the weekend, the right-hander has thrown two scoreless innings against the San Francisco Giants. In those appearances, he allowed just two baserunners and collected four strikeouts.
“Yeah, 100%,” Díaz said when asked if he feels as good as he has all season. “I’ve been able to throw strikes. That was my problem and concern. I wasn’t throwing my fastball for strike. Now I’m able to command my fastball pretty good. When I command my fastball, my slider plays up. So I feel really good right now.”
Díaz’s success is coming after an uneven rehab assignment with Triple-A Oklahoma City that drew some criticism from manager Dave Roberts. The three-time All-Star gave up five runs in his second-to-last appearance and was reminded that he needed to pitch better.
Díaz bounced back with a scoreless effort after working on some adjustments with Comets pitching coaches Ryan Dennick and David Anderson. It’s still early, but Díaz believes the changes have helped him regain command of his fastball, which had been an issue throughout the season.
“I think my mechanics are better,” Díaz said. “After my rough game in Triple-A, I sat down with the Triple-A pitching coach to see what was the problem. We found I wasn’t moving my hips the right way, so we started working on that.
Díaz further noted his slider is back to being the devastating secondary pitch that he has become known for in his career.
“Yeah, right now it’s really good,” Díaz said. “It’s going down and away. I’ve been able to throw my fastball glove side, and if I throw my fastball glove side, [the slider] will play up in the same path.”
Edwin Díaz benefiting from new role
Prior to rejoining the Dodgers, Roberts made it clear that Díaz would not be returning to the closer role anytime soon as a way to ease him back into action. Both of his appearances against the Giants came in low-leverage situations, and Díaz believes that approach has helped him thrive so far.
“Yeah, yeah. I have an open mind. I’m in the situation right now where I need to help this team to win,” Díaz explained. “Whenever Doc puts me in the game, in any situation, I will do my job. And I feel good. I just want to keep climbing the ladder and finish the season strong.”

item.title: [cubbiescrib.com] Dodgers could offer Cubs perfectly-timed solution to looming Ian Happ farewell
item.dc:creator: Jordan Campbell
item.description: At the very least, it seems likely that the Chicago Cubs will let both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki test the free-agent waters this offseason. Between the two, Suzuki makes sense for the Cubs to sign to a long-term deal, but he's positioned to be one of the best hitters available. item.content:encoded:
At the very least, it seems likely that the Chicago Cubs will let both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki test the free-agent waters this offseason. Between the two, Suzuki makes sense for the Cubs to sign to a long-term deal, but he's positioned to be one of the best hitters available.
Even if Suzuki does return to the Cubs next season, there' the question of replacing Happ. Not to mention, as a whole, the offense could be without Carson Kelly, Michael Conforto, and Tyrone Taylor next season. Pitching is going to be the focus for the Cubs during the offseason, but they can't ignore the position-player side of the roster.
If the Cubs are going to make an addition of consequence to their starting lineup this offseason, chances are it will be in the outfield. That is where things get interesting for the Cubs, considering the rise of Josiah Hartshorn and Kane Kepley this season. Hartshorn and Kepley have both finished the 2026 season with Double-A Knoxville, and while it would aggressive for what the Cubs typically do, one of the two could find their way to Wrigley Field by the end of the 2027 season.
Not to mention, Matt Shaw and Pedro Ramirez could be options, and Ethan Conrad still figures to be involved in the long-term outlook in the outfield.
But given that the Cubs are in the middle of a contention window, it makes sense for them to look for a stopgap in the outfield for the 2027 season. While the free-agent market is thin, the trade market could point them in the direction of the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Teoscar Hernández could give Cubs exactly the stopgap they need if they move on from Ian Happ
FanSided's Pat Ragazzo takes an early look at offseason trade candidates, and among the names mentioned is Dodgers outfielder Teoscar Hernández. While the Dodgers doubled down on Hernández's role at the start of September, and he responded a resurgent month, conventional wisdom points to him being someone LA would be willing to move this offseason. Especially since Josue De Paula looks ready for an expanded role next year.
Hernández is owed over $22 next season, and carries a $15 million club option for the 2028 season. The option also includes a $6.5 million buyout. For a team that has a short-term need in the outfield with over $100 million coming off the books after the season, Hernández wouldn't be that crazy of an option for the Cubs.
The concern is that Hernández's resurgence this month could be a blip. Overall, his numbers have trended in the wrong direction over the last two years, and that could position him to be massively overpaid next season. Ultimately, that could be the reason why the Cubs steer clear of the veteran outfielder in trade talks. But if they are willing to take a gamble, this could be a move to watch for during the offseason.

Tras otro día productivo en su progresión de bateo, Ohtani (bíceps derecho, rodilla izquierda) se sigue perfilando a ser activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días durante la próxima serie de los Dodgers contra los Padres, informó el d
item.content:encoded:
Existe ‘buena posibilidad’ de que Ohtani sea activado en la serie Padres-Dodgers
This browser does not support the video element.
LOS ÁNGELES -- Podría no pasar tanto tiempo antes de que Shohei Ohtani esté de regreso para encabezar la alineación de los Dodgers.
Tras otro día productivo en su progresión de bateo, Ohtani (bíceps derecho, rodilla izquierda) se sigue perfilando a ser activado de la lista de lesionados de 15 días durante la próxima serie de los Dodgers contra los Padres, informó el dirigente Dave Roberts tras la victoria del sábado por la noche 10-4 sobre los Gigantes en el Dodger Stadium.
"Hay una buena posiblidad de que lo veamos en la próxima serie", expresó Roberts.
El paso de Ohtani a la lista de lesionados de 15 días es retroactivo al 8 de septiembre, lo que significa que es elegible para ser activado el miércoles, el segundo encuentro de la última serie en casa de los bicampeones contra los Frailes. Regresará estrictamente como bateador, debido a que está descartado para lanzar.
Luego de comenzar una progresión de bateo el martes, Ohtani ya avanzó a batear frente a la máquina Trajekt, la cual simula enfrentar a verdaderos lanzadores. Salió sintiéndose bien tras realizar entre 30 y 40 swings el sábado, indicó Roberts. Ohtani también corrió las bases mientras la escuadra de Los Ángeles realizaba las prácticas de bateo en el terreno.
Ohtani registró OPS de .902 y encabezó el equipo con 30 jonrones antes de que sus persistentes lesiones en el bíceps derecho y la rodilla izquierda lo obligaran a apartarse. En sus 24 encuentros antes de ingresar a la lista de lesionados, que coincidió con un intento de intensificar su trabajo en el montículo, Ohtani bateó .198 (de 96-19) con 34 ponches en 96 turnos.
Si Ohtani regresa cuando sea elegible el miércoles, solo contará con cinco partidos de temporada regular para volverse a acoplar a la acción de las Grandes Ligas antes de la postemporada.
Los Dodgers han estado sin Ohtani en el lineup en 15 de sus últimos 16 compromisos, pero han encontrado su ritmo incluso sin su mejor bateador, consiguiendo marca de 13-3 en ese trecho.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] One stat defines just how dominant Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been for Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Evan Roberts
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers starting rotation is so good collectively when they are healthy that it's sometimes difficult to focus on the individuals' accomplishments. As a fan, it's easy to just look at the starting unit of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Shohei Ohtani as one. But Yamamoto's latest feat stands out even relative to this dominant group of pitchers. Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been dominant this season Yamamoto's most recent start came on S
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers starting rotation is so good collectively when they are healthy that it's sometimes difficult to focus on the individuals' accomplishments.
As a fan, it's easy to just look at the starting unit of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, and Shohei Ohtani as one. But Yamamoto's latest feat stands out even relative to this dominant group of pitchers.
Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto has been dominant this season
Yamamoto's most recent start came on September 15 against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. It was yet another ho-hum performance by the Dodgers ace. He picked up the win going seven scoreless innings, while allowing just one hit. He only walked two batters while striking out seven. Yamamoto lowered his career WHIP to 0.96, which is officially the best WHIP ever by a pitcher their first 75 career starts.
Yamamoto outpaced 2025 National League Cy Young Award-winner — and perhaps future Dodgers pitcher in Paul Skenes — as well as former member of LA's pitching staff, Walker Buehler. Behind Yamamoto, Skenes, and Buehler are Seattle Mariners All-Star starter Bryan Woo and Tampa Bay Rays right-hander Drew Rasmussen.
Not only does Yamamoto have the best WHIP ever through his first 75 games, but he's allowed the third-fewest runs in MLB history by a pitcher through that same span (trailing only Rasmussen and Skenes).
Opposing hitters are hitting .192/.252/.310 against Yamamoto through those 75 starts -- that is the lowest batting average against of any pitcher since 1974 (when that data became available). It's also the lowest on-base percentage, the fifth-lowest slugging percentage, and the second-lowest OPS.
Below is a list of fewest hits allowed in MLB history by a pitcher in their first 75 starts. There's a lot of familiar names on that list.
| Pitcher | Hits Allowed |
|---|---|
| 1. Tony Gonsolin (LAD) | 264 |
| 2. Freddy Peralta (MIL) | 270 |
| 3. Drew Rasmussen (TB) | 284 |
| T-4. Cristian Javier (HOU) | 287 |
| T-4. Edward Cabrera (MIA) | 287 |
| 6. Triston McKenzie (CLE) | 295 |
| 7. Jack Flaherty (STL) | 299 |
| T-8. Yoshinobu Yamamoto (LAD) | 305 |
| T-8. Shohei Ohtani (LAA) | 305 |
| 10. Tyler Glasnow (LAD) | 313 |
Yamamoto has clearly been worth every penny since he signed that mega-deal with the Dodgers. It's nice to be able to point to his historic regular season success as well as his historic postseason success. Yamamoto is slowly building up a Hall of Fame résumé through his first three Major League seasons.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] This day in Dodgers history: L.A. Coliseum, Sandy Koufax and Clayton Kershaw
item.dc:creator: Staff Writer
item.description: This day in Los Angeles Dodgers history saw the end of an era at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, plus Sandy Koufax and Clayton Kershaw reach individual milestones. item.content:encoded:
This day in Los Angeles Dodgers history saw the end of an era at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, plus Sandy Koufax and Clayton Kershaw reach individual milestones.
On Sept. 20, 1961, the Dodgers came away with a 3-2 walk-off win against the Chicago Cubs in 13 innings. The game was notable in that Koufax not only pitched all 13 innings but it was the Dodgers’ final time playing at the L.A. Coliseum.
It was their home since moving from Brooklyn for the start of the 1958 season and until Dodger Stadium opened on April 10, 1962.
En route to pitching a complete game, Koufax finished with 15 strikeouts to earn his 18th win of the season.
Although that marked the Dodgers’ final time playing at the Coliseum, their 1961 season concluded with a nine-game road trip comprised of series against the St. Louis Cardinals, Pittsburgh Pirates and Cubs.
The Dodgers went 89-65, good for second place in the National League. They finished four games back of the Cincinnati Reds, who lost in the World Series to the New York Yankees.
On Sept. 20, 1966, Koufax was part of another memorable performance as he became the first NL pitcher in 31 years with back-to-back seasons of at least 25 victories.
Koufax reached the milestone with a complete game in the Dodgers 11-1 win over the Philadelphia Phillies at Dodger Stadium. The left-hander had 26 wins in 1965 and 27 in 1966, which wound up being his final season.
On Sept. 20, 2011, Kershaw became the Dodgers’ first 20-game winner since Ramon Martinez accomplished the feat in 1990. Kershaw pitched 7.1 innings against the San Francisco Giants to earn his 20th win.
Dodgers returned to Coliseum
On March 29, 2008, the Dodgers faced defending World Series champion Boston Red Sox in front of 115,300 fans for an exhibition game at the L.A. Memorial Coliseum. It was held to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Dodgers franchise moving from Brooklyn to Los Angeles.
The crowd represented the largest ever for a baseball game, surpassing the approximately 114,000 fans that were in attendance when the Australian national team played an American services team during the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne.

item.title: [cbssports.com] Dodgers eye sweep of Giants behind surging Mookie Betts
item.dc:creator: FLM
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers will continue getting their house in order when they face the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon to complete the Dodgers' next-to-last home series of the regular season. Los Angeles will use a bullpen game Sunday when it seeks a three-game series sweep, while the Giants will send left-hander Matt Wilkinson (1-3, 4.58 ERA) to the mound for his first appearance against the Dodgers. Los Angeles has a lot of uncertainty heading into its 14th consecutive playoff appearan
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers will continue getting their house in order when they face the San Francisco Giants on Sunday afternoon to complete the Dodgers' next-to-last home series of the regular season.
Los Angeles will use a bullpen game Sunday when it seeks a three-game series sweep, while the Giants will send left-hander Matt Wilkinson (1-3, 4.58 ERA) to the mound for his first appearance against the Dodgers.
Los Angeles has a lot of uncertainty heading into its 14th consecutive playoff appearance -- including the rotation because Blake Snell is working through groin discomfort -- while the offense has Shohei Ohtani (biceps inflammation, knee soreness) and Andy Pages (left hand fracture) nearing a return from the injured list.
The revival of Mookie Betts, along with the arrival of Josue De Paula from the minor leagues, has brought renewed energy after a mid-summer swoon.
The Dodgers still do not have a return date for Ohtani, with Betts the latest to claim the star's leadoff spot. Betts had two home runs among his three hits as the leadoff hitter Friday, then returned to the top spot Saturday and went 4-for-4 with three doubles and a walk. He has 10 hits over his past three games.
"The main thing is doing it when it counts," Betts said. "So right now, we just keep laying the foundation, and then when playoffs come, just need it to show up (offensively)."
Betts had an RBI single in the second inning and an RBI double in the fourth Saturday as the Dodgers earned a 10-4 victory over the Giants.
"He's not a chase guy anyway, but he's cut that down considerably," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "The quality of contact is considerably higher. And then now you've got that attitude, that confidence, that we're used to seeing with Mookie."
The Dodgers' Will Smith also is rounding into form after missing three months with neck inflammation. Smith returned at the start of September and has three home runs over his past nine games, including one in each of the past two games.
Smith started consecutive games Friday and Saturday for the third time since he returned, although he is expected to be used off the bench, if at all, on Sunday.
The Giants have their own injury concerns. Ace Logan Webb was the latest to see his season end early, due to a blister on his right middle finger.
On Saturday, first baseman Bryce Eldridge missed his second consecutive game with a head laceration. The 6-foot-7 rookie bumped his head on a low overhang at the team hotel.
"He's still feeling the implications of that deal," Giants manager Tony Vitello said Saturday. "It's kind of a weird spot in the hotel. I checked it out. (Friday) it was a little bit more about just his comfort. But now, stemming from last night and this morning, those guys have been monitoring him like crazy. Just some lingering effects."
Giants rookie Victor Bericoto hit a two-run home run Saturday in his second game since returning from the injured list and now has five homers in 35 career games.
With a win Sunday, the Dodgers can earn their first three-game sweep over the Giants since April 2024. Los Angeles leads the season series 5-4, with one game remaining in L.A. and three games at San Francisco to end the regular season.

item.title: [Dodger Blue] Dave Roberts acknowledges Dodgers still have big need for postseason
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Abdón Ibarra

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers clinched their 13th National League West title in the last 14 seasons, and now all that remains to do is stay in front of the Atlanta Braves down the stretch to secure a first-round bye.
“It’s always helpful in the sense of giving your guys a break to reset. But given all the tax and where our guys are health-wise, to get that week would be huge,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts recently said. “We’ve still got to play well to finish out the season to get to that point. There’s a lot of people that could use the break.”
The Dodgers have a four-game lead over the Braves for the second seed in the NL. L.A. needs to finish with a better record than the Braves by virtue of not holding the head-to-head tiebreaker.
The top seed in the NL is within reach for the Dodgers, but they do not control their own destiny due to trailing the Milwaukee Brewers in the standings. Furthermore, the Dodgers also don’t have the tiebreaker over the Brewers.
Securing home-field advantage throughout the postseason would certainly be of value, but finishing as one of the top two division winners in the NL is of greater importance.
Some of the notable injuries the Dodgers are dealing with include Shohei Ohtani, Edgardo Henriquez, Andy Pages, Will Klein and, most recently, Blake Snell.
The Wild Card Series begins Tuesday, Sept. 29, while the NL Division Series starts Saturday, Oct. 3.
Pages and Ohtani are expected to be activated prior to the regular season concluding, and there is optimism Snell will avoid going on the injured list.
Henriquez is eligible to return on the same day the Wild Card round begins. Meanwhile, Klein can’t return until the NLDS starts. It is not a given that the Dodgers would elect to have Klein on their postseason roster given his two-month absence, but they would still prefer to have the option.
Dodgers postseason outlook
Should the Dodgers remain the No. 2 seed in the NL postseason bracket, they would face the Wild Card winner of the matchup between the third division champion and sixth-place team. However, who that could be is still very much in question in part because of a late surge from the San Diego Padres.
The Chicago Cubs, Philadelphia Phillies and Padres are all in a dead heat and mathematically possible of slotting into any order as the three Wild Card teams.

item.title: [FanSided] Edwin Díaz’s brilliant return should make Dodgers haters very, very nervous
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Only the Los Angeles Dodgers could have a $69 million All-Star closer as a potential hidden weapon ahead of the postseason. Such a thing shouldn’t be possible, but the Dodgers aren’t most teams. item.content:encoded:
Only the Los Angeles Dodgers could have a $69 million All-Star closer as a potential hidden weapon ahead of the postseason.
Such a thing shouldn’t be possible, but the Dodgers aren’t most teams. Friday night’s blowout win over the Giants presented what’s been a rare sight this year: Edwin Díaz taking the mound in the ninth inning. The 32-year-old has missed much of the season with elbow and neck problems, and the 8-2 rout marked his first outing since Aug. 17.
Díaz pitching a scoreless ninth in September is exactly what Dodgers fans envisioned when they added the three-time All-Star this past offseason. However, manager Dave Roberts confirmed that Díaz, who had recorded an 11.85 ERA and allowed 10 walks in his first 14.2 innings, will not move back into the closer role.
In fact, Roberts admitted he would not have used the veteran reliever on Friday night if not for the team's six-run lead. To his credit, Díaz worked around a two-out single, and his fastball averaged 97.6 mph, which MLB's Sarah Wexler reported was up 1.3 mph from his season average.
“I think we just want to see him throw the baseball the way he's capable of,” Roberts said. “And you’re talking about nine games, so you're talking three or four outings to evaluate, and that should be adequate.”
The story was much the same on Saturday: L.A. calling on Diaz in a six-run game, and Diaz striking out two batters with just one baserunner in a scoreless inning — all while looking much more like the guy the Dodgers thought they were acquiring this offseason.
Could Edwin Díaz actually help the Los Angeles Dodgers in the postseason?
If the postseason began Sunday, the Dodgers would be the NL’s No. 2 seed and have a first-round bye. They’d then host the highest remaining seed in the NLDS, which would either be the NL East-leading Braves or the No. 6 seed (the Phillies held that spot entering Sunday, though they are one game back of the No. 4 Cubs and No. 5 Padres).
Wexler wrote that Díaz is competing for a spot on the playoff roster, which isn’t overly surprising to anyone familiar with Roberts’ mindset. Financial commitments and a player’s Baseball-Reference pages only matter so much, and the Dodgers have three championships in the last six years to prove it.
Roberts, who took over the Dodgers ahead of the 2016 season, has spent the last decade proving he’s not afraid to bench underperforming players or go with the hot hand. If Díaz returns to his earlier form and is dreadful over the team’s final seven games, it's difficult to imagine he’d be a lock to make the 26-man playoff roster.
The reality is that neither Roberts nor the Dodgers know what they’ll get from Díaz, who already has four games where he's given up at least three runs. He’s been worth -1.2 bWAR in 17 games, and he allowed five runs, three walks and a hit by pitch during a recent Triple-A outing during his rehab stint.
Personally, we’re skeptical about Díaz making a significant positive difference if he makes the postseason roster. Two low-stress outings don't make up for an entire season's worth of dysfunction. But the velocity is now creeping back up into the high 90s, and that's an awfully promising sign. We need to see him keep doing it over the final week of the regular season, but if he can, that could answer this team's most pressing question entering October.
Díaz has silenced his critics in the past, most notably after an ugly first season with the Mets in 2019. Hey, we were willing to own our prediction that the Nationals would lose at least 110 games. Prove us wrong, Edwin!
